headline: Australia's top court hears social media ban challenge

sources.title: Major test for Australia's social media ban begins in High Court (BBC)
Australia's highest court hears challenges to social media ban for children (Associated Press)
Reddit blasts 'inept' Australian social media ban as challenge airs in court (Reuters)
High Court to consider whether under-16s social media ban is unconstitutional (ABC News)
Australia's High Court hears bid to overturn under-16s social media ban (Al Jazeera)

chunks.text: Australia was the first country to [[ban]] social media for children under 16. The law {{kicked in}} on December 10, 2025. On November 3, 2026, it faced its first test at the High Court, Australia's top court. Reddit, an [[online forum]] covered by the ban, and an Australian [[online rights]] group brought a [[legal challenge]]. They want judges to {{strike down}} the ban.

verbs.correct: To start to have an effect
verbs.wrong: To be discussed in a court
verbs.why: The new rules kick in on Monday. My headache pills kick in after about an hour. The law kicked in on December 10, 2025.

verbs.wrong: To explain a law to children
verbs.why: Judges sometimes strike down very old laws. Courts strike down rules that break the constitution. Reddit and an online rights group want the judges to strike down the ban.

chunks.text: Both say the ban breaks Australia's [[constitution]], its document of basic laws. They say the constitution protects a freedom to discuss politics, even though it does not state that freedom directly. Reddit's lawyer said the ban {{cuts young people off}} from the most important way to communicate today. He said the law does not explain how sites should {{turn children away}}. He added that much [[content]] can be seen without {{logging in}}.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from reaching something
verbs.wrong: To make someone pay to use a site
verbs.why: Heavy snow cuts our town off from the highway. A long illness cuts him off from his friends. Reddit's lawyer said the ban cuts young people off from the most important way to communicate.

verbs.correct: To refuse to let someone enter
verbs.wrong: To send someone a warning notice
verbs.why: The club turns away anyone under 21. Busy restaurants turn people away on Saturday nights. Reddit's lawyer said the law does not explain how sites should turn children away.

verbs.correct: To enter a website with your account
verbs.wrong: To write a comment on a website
verbs.why: I log in to my bank's website every week. You log in with a name and a password. Reddit's lawyer said much content can be seen without logging in.

chunks.text: The group's case started with two 15-year-olds, who later {{dropped out}}. The Associated Press reported concerns that they could owe [[legal costs]] if the case failed. One of them, now 16, {{spoke out}} to reporters, calling the law a step toward [[censorship]]. Nearly 5 million accounts have been [[blocked]]. But government research in March showed 7 in 10 children under 16 {{held on to}} their accounts. Many parents supported the law when it took effect.

verbs.correct: To leave something before it ends
verbs.wrong: To request more time in court
verbs.why: Some runners drop out when the weather is too hot. He drops out of every class he starts. Two teenagers in the case later dropped out.

verbs.correct: To say publicly what you think is wrong
verbs.wrong: To answer questions from a judge
verbs.why: Some workers speak out when they see unfair pay. She speaks out about problems at her school. One of the teenagers, now 16, spoke out against the law outside the court.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose it
verbs.wrong: To report something to an adult
verbs.why: Many people hold on to old phones for years. Some fans hold on to their tickets after a game. Government research showed that 7 in 10 children under 16 held on to their accounts.

chunks.text: The government {{pushed back}} in court. Its lawyer said children are more [[vulnerable]] than adults to social media's [[addictive]] [[features]]. The [[communications minister]] said she was {{standing up for}} children's right to be free from harm. The government has doubled the [[top fine]] for breaking the rules to 99 million Australian dollars, {{stepping up}} pressure on social media companies. [[Lawmakers]] from Britain to Malaysia have been {{rolling out}} similar rules. The judges can {{throw out}} the challenge or cancel the law. When the two-day [[hearing]] opened, it was not clear when they would decide.

verbs.wrong: To start a new case in court
verbs.why: Workers push back when the company cuts their pay. Parents often push back when a school changes its rules. The government pushed back in court and defended the law.
Good friends stand up for each other. She stands up for her students at every meeting. The communications minister said she was standing up for children's right to be free from harm.

verbs.correct: To increase an effort or pressure
verbs.why: The police step up their patrols before big games. Schools step up pressure on students before exams. The government has stepped up pressure on social media companies by doubling the top fine.

verbs.wrong: To argue about a plan in public
verbs.why: Phone companies roll out new features every year. The city rolls out its new bus plan in stages. Lawmakers from Britain to Malaysia have been rolling out similar rules.

verbs.wrong: To hear a case for a second time
verbs.why: Judges throw out cases when there is no evidence. Courts throw out weak lawsuits every year. The judges can throw out the challenge or cancel the law.

mainIdea.s: Reddit and an Australian group are asking the country's top court to end the ban on social media for under-16s. They say it limits free communication, while the government says it protects children.
mainIdea.why: Reddit and an online rights group want the judges to strike down the ban. The government pushed back and says it is standing up for children.

mainIdea.s: Australia's highest judges are hearing a case against the teen rule, and the government itself brought it. Officials now believe their law has failed, so they want it canceled as soon as possible.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Reddit and an online rights group brought the case. The government pushed back in court and is defending the law.

mainIdea.s: Australian officials have decided to raise the minimum age for using apps from 16 to 18. Parents welcomed the plan in a national survey, and the new limit will begin in every state next summer.
mainIdea.why: No new age limit was announced. Reddit and an online rights group want the judges to strike down the ban, and the government is defending it.

tf.s: Reddit and an online rights group want the court to strike down the ban.
tf.why: They brought a legal challenge and say the ban breaks Australia's constitution.

tf.s: The government did not push back against the challenge in court.
tf.why: The government pushed back. Its lawyer said children are more vulnerable than adults to social media's addictive features.

tf.s: The two teenagers stayed in the case until the hearing.
tf.why: Both teenagers dropped out of the case before the hearing. One of them, now 16, still spoke out against the law outside the court.

tf.s: The challengers say the ban cuts young people off from communication.
tf.why: Reddit's lawyer said the ban cuts young people off from the most important way to communicate.

tf.s: Many children under 16 have held on to their accounts despite the ban.
tf.why: Government research released in March showed that 7 in 10 children under 16 held on to their accounts.

tf.s: The judges made their decision on the first day of the hearing.
tf.why: When the hearing opened, it was not clear how long the judges would take to decide whether to throw out the challenge.

lines.text: Did you hear about the court case over Australia's social media ban?
I thought that law {{kicked in}} in December 2025.
It did. Now Reddit and an online rights group want the top court to {{strike it down}}.
So they finally get their [[day in court]]. What's their argument?
They say the ban {{cuts young people off}} from the main way people communicate today.
The ban is meant to protect kids. [[That said]], lots of them {{held on to}} their accounts.
[[For sure]]. Government research put the number at 7 in 10.
So what does the government say?
It {{pushed back}} in court. The communications minister says she's {{standing up for}} a child's right to be free from harm.
That's a strong argument. Kids are more vulnerable online.
[[On the other hand]], the challengers say the law [[goes too far]].
Weren't there two teenagers in the case?
Yes, but they {{dropped out}}. One is 16 now, and he still {{spoke out}} against the law.
Seven judges. They can {{throw out}} the challenge or cancel the law.
Other countries must be watching closely.
They are. Lawmakers from Britain to Malaysia have been {{rolling out}} similar rules.

expressions.def: Used to agree strongly with what someone said

expressions.def: Used to give a different side of the same question
